position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Instead, conduct a low‑cost choice experiment (as proposed) to test whether homeowners value time‑saving multipurpose functionality (T1) or status and prestige (T2). Use the results to decide whether to develop a differentiated product or maintain focus on existing markets. The €20,000 budget and 12‑week timeline are sufficient for a credible test.

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must address consumer demand, willingness to pay, and feasibility of reaching individual buyers.
Must consider existing dealer network and any existing consumer sales channels.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., small‑holder farming, hobby gardening, or residential landscaping) using existing tractor engineering.
2) Expand into consumer markets without differentiation, offering tractors directly to individual buyers through dealers or new retail channels.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on existing farm, combine, and industrial equipment markets and dealer network.

T1.claim: Homeowners will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they view them as a time‑saving, multipurpose tool for yard work, and they are willing to pay a premium for integrated design and dealer support.
T1.who_benefits: Homeowners gain efficiency and convenience; Deere gains higher margins through premium pricing and dealer commissions.
T1.why_behaviour_changes: If homeowners perceive a tractor as a single purchase that solves multiple yard tasks, they will prioritize it over separate tools and be willing to pay more for a single, reliable solution.
T1.how_value_is_captured: Deere captures value by selling tractors at higher prices, earning dealer commissions, and potentially bundling attachments, creating a differentiated revenue stream from existing dealer network.
assumptions: Homeowners in 1962 have sufficient disposable income to afford a lawn and garden tractor.
They value time savings and are willing to invest in a single, multipurpose tool.
Deere can design a tractor that is easy to operate and maintain for non‑farm users.
predictions: Surveyed homeowners will indicate willingness to pay at least 15% above the price of a comparable garden tool for a tractor that performs multiple tasks.
Dealer surveys will show increased interest in stocking lawn and garden tractors if they promise higher margins and reduced training requirements.
T1.first_claim: Homeowners will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they view them as a time‑saving, multipurpose tool for yard work, and they are willing to pay a premium for integrated design and dealer support.

T2.claim: Homeowners will adopt lawn and garden tractors because they view them as a status symbol and a modern, convenient way to show off their yard, and they are willing to pay a premium for design and brand prestige.
T2.who_benefits: Homeowners gain a sense of modern lifestyle and social status; Deere gains premium pricing and brand loyalty, leveraging its existing dealer network to capture higher margins.
T2.why_behaviour_changes: If homeowners perceive a tractor as a visible, desirable product that signals sophistication, they will prioritize it over functional-only tools and be willing to pay more for aesthetics and brand reputation.
T2.how_value_is_captured: Deere captures value by selling tractors at premium prices, offering limited editions or design variations, and potentially bundling accessories that enhance status, creating a differentiated revenue stream from its existing dealer network.
assumptions: Homeowners in 1962 value social status and modern lifestyle as part of their consumer identity.
They are willing to allocate a portion of their discretionary income to products that signal status.
Deere can design tractors that are visually appealing and distinctive without compromising core engineering.
predictions: Surveyed homeowners will indicate willingness to pay at least 20% above the price of a comparable garden tool for a tractor with unique design features.
Dealer surveys will show increased interest in stocking tractors if they are marketed as status items, not just functional tools.

X1.name: Choice Experiment: Time‑Saving vs Status Messaging
X1.method: Online survey presenting two product descriptions of a hypothetical lawn and garden tractor, each emphasizing a different value proposition: (1) time‑saving multipurpose tool with integrated attachments; (2) status‑enhancing design and brand prestige. Participants indicate willingness to pay a premium (percentage above a baseline price) and choose which description they would select. The test is run with 300 U.S. homeowners recruited via an online panel, balanced across age, gender, and region. Each participant sees one of the two descriptions.
X1.sample: 300 U.S. homeowners, recruited via an online panel, balanced across age, gender, and region.
X1.measure: 1) Willingness to pay premium (percentage above baseline price) for each description. 2) Choice: which description they would select (Time‑Saving vs Status).

prediction_by_theory.T1: Participants will show higher willingness to pay and select the time‑saving description, because they value multipurpose functionality and are willing to pay a premium for integrated tools.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Participants will show higher willingness to pay and select the status description, because they value social prestige and are willing to pay a premium for distinctive design and brand reputation.

X1.decision_rule: If the average willingness to pay premium for the time‑saving description exceeds the premium for the status description by at least 10 percentage points (e.g., 20% vs 10%), we conclude T1 is better supported. If the status description premium exceeds the time‑saving premium by at least 10 percentage points, we conclude T2 is better supported. If the difference is less than 10 percentage points, the evidence is inconclusive.

position.recommendation: Do not invest in a differentiated consumer proposition at this time. Instead, conduct a low‑cost survey test (as proposed) to empirically compare homeowner willingness to pay and motivation for a multipurpose versus status‑oriented tractor concept. If the test confirms the multipurpose concept drives higher premium willingness and time‑saving motivation, proceed to develop a differentiated consumer line; otherwise,

frame.objective: Determine whether there is sufficient evidence from public sources available in mid-1962 to justify Deere & Company investing in a differentiated consumer proposition for a specific use case, leveraging its tractor engineering.
constraints: Limited to public sources published before mid-1962; no internal company data.
Test budget of €20,000 and 12‑week timeline for any proposed experiment.
Evidence must address consumer demand, willingness to pay, and feasibility of reaching individual buyers.
Must consider existing dealer network and any existing consumer sales channels.
alternatives: 1) Develop a differentiated consumer proposition targeting a specific use case (e.g., small‑holder farming, hobby gardening, or residential landscaping) using existing tractor engineering.
2) Expand into consumer markets without differentiation, offering tractors directly to individual buyers through dealers or new retail channels.
3) No expansion: continue focusing exclusively on existing farm, combine, and industrial equipment markets and dealer network.

X1.name: Consumer Preference Survey for Lawn and Garden Tractors
X1.method: Online survey with randomized presentation of two tractor concepts: (1) a multipurpose, time‑saving tractor described as "ideal for small‑holder farming, hobby gardening, and yard work" (T1); (2) a status‑oriented tractor described as "a modern, convenient way to show off your yard and signal sophistication" (T2). Participants are asked to indicate willingness to pay a premium (percentage above a comparable garden tool) and their primary motivation (time‑saving/multipurpose vs. status).
X1.sample: 500 U.S. homeowners aged 25‑65, recruited via an online panel, balanced for region and household income.
X1.measure: Average premium willingness to pay (percentage) and primary motivation (time‑saving/multipurpose vs. status) for each concept.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher average premium for the multipurpose concept and higher proportion citing time‑saving/multipurpose as primary motivation.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher average premium for the status concept and higher proportion citing status as primary motivation.

X1.decision_rule: If the average premium for the multipurpose concept exceeds the average premium for the status concept by at least 10 percentage points AND the proportion citing time‑saving/multipurpose is at least 55% of respondents, then T1 is supported. If the average premium for the status concept exceeds the average premium for the multipurpose concept by at least 10 percentage points AND the proportion citing status is at least 55% of respondents, then T2 is supported. If neither condition is met, both theories remain uncertain.

arguments.method: Online survey with randomized presentation of two tractor concepts: (1) a multipurpose, time‑saving tractor described as "ideal for small‑holder farming, hobby gardening, and yard work" (T1); (2) a status‑oriented tractor described as "a modern, convenient way to show off your yard and signal sophistication" (T2). Participants are asked to indicate willingness to pay a premium (percentage above a comparable garden tool) and their primary motivation (time‑saving/multipurpose vs. status).
arguments.sample: 500 U.S. homeowners aged 25‑65, recruited via an online panel, balanced for region and household income.
arguments.measure: Average premium willingness to pay (percentage) and primary motivation (time‑saving/multipurpose vs. status) for each concept.

prediction_by_theory.T1: Higher average premium for the multipurpose concept and higher proportion citing time‑saving/multipurpose as primary motivation.
prediction_by_theory.T2: Higher average premium for the status concept and higher proportion citing status as primary motivation.

arguments.decision_rule: If the average premium for the multipurpose concept exceeds the average premium for the status concept by at least 10 percentage points AND the proportion citing time‑saving/multipurpose is at least 55% of respondents, then T1 is supported. If the average premium for the status concept exceeds the average premium for the multipurpose concept by at least 10 percentage points AND the proportion citing status is at least 55% of respondents, then T2 is supported. If neither condition is met, both theories remain uncertain.
